selection: First ten saved errors, ordered by comparison ID; no model or gold-label changes.
scope: Only the supplied claim and older passage were reviewed. Eight of these ten pairs come from the same source paper, so these counts are not a representative estimate of all error types.
summary: Six reviewed errors have gold insufficient_evidence: five were predicted distinct and one overlapping. These excerpts generally state aims, definitions, or questions without results. Two clear overlapping cases were missed where a specific numerical result restated a broader finding. One case concerns delivery-model specificity, and one gold overlap judgment remains ambiguous from the excerpts.

errors.evidence_observation: Both excerpts discuss positive MAP outcomes, but only the claim specifies scattered-site delivery. The older passage does not establish whether its MAP used the same delivery model; broad outcome similarity can obscure that distinction.

The claim links particular substance use disorders to lower housing attainment. The older passage describes HF outcomes and an ongoing alcohol issue, without explicitly reporting that association or the opioid/methamphetamine result. The supplied excerpts leave the rationale for the gold overlap judgment ambiguous; the gold label is retained.

Both excerpts report reductions in alcohol-related harms and seizures. The claim adds specific rates and a year-to-year comparison; treating those details as a new main finding misses the shared outcome.
The older passage already reports reduced acute and social harms from MAPs. The claim supplies narrower outcomes and numerical changes, but the central reduction in harms overlaps.
The older passage gives the MAP rationale and study objectives, not findings. It cannot establish whether the reported changes in harms and seizures were present or absent.
The older passage defines MAP services without reporting health, nonbeverage alcohol, survival-behavior, or violence outcomes. Missing outcome evidence was treated as a distinct finding.
The older passage says length of stay was investigated as a predictor, but provides no result. The shared outcome topics do not supply enough evidence to compare the claimed improvements.
The older passage states that MAPs aim to reduce harms; it does not show that they did so. Similar wording about health and social benefits was treated as evidence of overlapping results.
The older passage states a harm-reduction aim without outcome findings. It does not establish whether the claimed positive health and social outcomes overlap or differ.
The older passage describes general harm-reduction support. It supplies no evidence about program gaps or out-of-program drinking, so it cannot establish a distinct contribution.
